summary:
Hungary's civil regime bars transgender people from correcting their legal gender. Administrative refusal became routine from 2018, and the barrier became explicit law in May 2020, when the government legislated by emergency decree during the COVID-19 pandemic to stop passports and identity cards from reflecting an acquired gender, including for people already legally recognised, while redefining nem (sex) in the civil code as immutable biological sex. Human Rights Watch records the 2020 provision as banning legal gender change for transgender and intersex people.

The practical consequence for a visitor is documentation. No domestic administrative route to correcting a gender marker is documented in this record, and a trans visitor should expect to enter, be screened and be recorded under the marker assigned at birth, carrying papers that may not match presentation. The 2021 child protection law separately bars legal gender change for people under 18, an under-18 gender-change ban argued under child-protection law.

Two rulings of the Court of Justice of the European Union bear on that exposure. On 13 March 2025, in case C-247/23 Deldits, on a reference from the Budapest High Court in an immigration matter, the Court held that Article 16 GDPR requires the national register authority to rectify recorded gender data where it has changed and no longer complies with the accuracy principle of Article 5(1)(d). In September 2024 the Court's Advocate General called on Hungarian authorities to correct a transgender refugee's gender marker in national registries. In April 2026 the Court found that the 2021 child protection law discriminated against and scapegoated LGBTI residents, and ruled that Orbán-era anti-LGBTQ laws breached EU rules on several levels, including Article 2 of the EU Treaty on founding values, which the source describes as an unprecedented finding against a founding value.

The political layer changed at the 12 April 2026 election, when Fidesz lost power and the Tisza party took 138 seats, ending 16 years of Viktor Orbán's rule. Tens of thousands marched in the 31st Budapest Pride in June 2026, the first held since Orbán was voted out, against the backdrop of the anti-LGBT laws adopted during his rule. Budapest Pride spokesperson Johanna Majercsik named restoration of the right to assembly as the most urgent outstanding issue and stated that anti-queer laws can be repealed only with a two-thirds majority, while the Tisza party's silence on LGBTQ+ rights under Péter Magyar has raised questions about the pace of change. No repeal of the 2020 legal gender recognition ban is documented in this record. In September 2026 Prime Minister Péter Magyar announced intent to repeal the ban on adoption by same-sex couples.

Relationship recognition runs through the partnership track rather than marriage. Registered partnerships for same-sex couples have been available since 1 July 2009, carrying the same rights as spouses except adoption, assisted reproduction and taking a surname, while same-sex marriage was banned by the 1 January 2012 constitution. A trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship should expect that regime to apply on any question of recognition.

Official hostility is documented across the period. The National Assembly's May 2020 resolution rejecting the Istanbul Convention attacked the treaty's measures as promoting "destructive gender ideologies" and "illegal migration"; in October 2020 Orbán said "gays are to leave our children alone". After a 2021 children's book by the Labrisz Lesbian Association, Fidesz launched a smear campaign confusing homosexuality with pedophilia, and the government-linked media giant Mediaworks published an article calling Labrisz pedophiles without proof. Labrisz won at first instance, but the Curia ruled in November 2022 that the article did not violate its right to good reputation and the case was appealed to the Constitutional Court. HRW's 2025 country chapter states that LGBT people continue to face discrimination and demonization.

Custody and screening carry their own exposure. A 2025 national report by the Hungarian Helsinki Committee and the Háttér Society, part of an EU-funded project on LGBTIQ detainees, documents the situation and rights of LGBTIQ people in Hungarian detention amid the current legal and political climate. In January 2018 the Court of Justice of the European Union ruled that asylum seekers may not be subjected by authorities to psychological tests in order to determine their sexual orientation.
tangentialFactors:
The April 2026 Court of Justice of the European Union ruling is described by its source as unprecedented because it found a breach of Article 2 of the EU Treaty, the founding-values provision, rather than only a technical breach of secondary rules. That finding arrived nine days after Hungarians voted in the election that ended Fidesz rule, so judicial and electoral pressure converged within a fortnight.

Repeal arithmetic is the main constraint on change. Budapest Pride's spokesperson stated in April 2026 that anti-queer laws can be undone with a two-thirds majority in the National Assembly, and the Tisza party held 138 seats after the 12 April 2026 vote, leaving the threshold and the party's own silence on LGBTQ+ rights as the open questions. Interviewees told France24 in June 2026 that they were very hopeful changes will be made, which is expectation rather than enacted law.

The record's hostility evidence is dated and specific rather than measured: a far-right party displayed a sign reading "The Parliament Does Not Want Any Deviants" and verbally abused attendees at Budapest Pride in 2014; the Curia's November 2022 ruling in the Labrisz case; the May 2020 Istanbul Convention resolution. No dated prevalence figure for trans-specific violence against visitors appears in this inventory, and no trans-specific killing rate is stated with a denominator, so no comparative risk ranking can be drawn from it.

The 31st Budapest Pride in June 2026 drew tens of thousands, a raw crowd count with no per-capita basis and no bearing on individual exposure at a border, a registry counter or in custody.
localsOnly:
Legal gender recognition is closed to residents as well as visitors: the May 2020 decree and the redefinition of nem as immutable biological sex apply to national records, and no administrative petition route is documented here. The Deldits judgment of 13 March 2025 puts an obligation on the national register authority under Article 16 GDPR to rectify recorded gender data that no longer complies with the accuracy principle of Article 5(1)(d), and the September 2024 Advocate General opinion concerned a transgender refugee's marker in the same registries.

Family law for residents: unregistered cohabitation has been recognised since 1996 for any couple, including same-sex couples, giving specified rights with inheritance only by testament and a widow's pension after 10 years. Registered partnerships run from 1 July 2009 with the rights of spouses except adoption, assisted reproduction and taking a surname; same-sex couples cannot adopt jointly, stepchild adoption is limited to married different-sex couples, and IVF and donor insemination are unavailable to lesbians in a registered partnership. A December 2020 constitutional amendment further banned adoption by same-sex couples and restricted single-parent adoption. In September 2026 Péter Magyar announced intent to repeal the same-sex adoption ban.

Assembly was the issue Budapest Pride itself flagged after the 12 April 2026 election, with Johanna Majercsik calling restoration of the right to assembly the most urgent matter. The 2025 Hungarian Helsinki Committee and Háttér Society report is the resident-facing document on LGBTIQ detainees, produced within an EU-funded project on Strengthening the rights of LGBTIQ detainees in the EU. The Labrisz litigation over the November 2022 Curia ruling remained appealed to the Constitutional Court at the close of this inventory.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: whether the Deldits rectification obligation of 13 March 2025 has been implemented in Hungarian registry practice is not stated by any source here, and no domestic administrative procedure following it is sourced.

Unresolved: whether the April 2026 Court of Justice of the European Union rulings on the 2021 child protection law and the wider anti-LGBT package have produced amendments, and whether the under-18 gender-change ban remains in force as of the latest source in this inventory, is not documented. The record's latest legal statements run to September 2026 and show announced intent, not enacted change.

Unresolved: no source here reports enforcement practice against trans visitors at Hungarian border or airport screening, so differential treatment at entry rests on the document rules alone rather than on observed screening incidents.

Unresolved: the inventory contains no trans-specific violence figure for Hungary with a stated denominator or period, so no comparison against the general homicide rate can be made and none is offered.
